question: The first violin ends Dvořáks "Symphony no. 2, Op. 4" on three notes. Which is the lowest one?

2.text:
In the B♭ major edition the whole orchestra closes the Finale on a
fermata B♭–D–F. The first violins get the closing arpeggiation of the
tonic triad, written in the treble as the familiar

    F – D – B♭

descending, B♭–D–F ascending, the coda of the Allegro vivace.  In
concert pitch that is the B♭–D–F of B♭ major in the top octave of the
instrument, i.e. in the first-violin staff the bottom note of the
figure is the written B♭ that lies on the first line of the treble,
B♭3 in scientific pitch, the tonic B♭ of the work, the lowest of the
three attacks of the closing arpeggiation.  It is the tonic B♭ that is
held as the final fermata of the symphony, the lowest member of the
final B♭–D–F triad that the first violins play.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The finale is in B flat major and the first violin finishes the coda with the
tonic arpeggio of the key.  On the paper it is written as the familiar
descending B flat – major arpeggio

    F  –  D  –  B♭

on the last beats of the movement, the F and D being the third and the
fifth of the tonic and the B♭ being the final down-beat of the piece.
Hence the third and last of the three pitches is the tonic itself, B♭,
the B♭ that is written in the violin part in the 3rd position / ≈ B♭3,
about the B♭ just below middle C, the final note of the Symphony No. 2
Op. 4. The B♭ is of course the lowest of the three pitches F-D-B♭ and
is the note on which the movement – and the Symphony – is closed.
